nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.question: What is the significance of timing in the application of nitrogen from digestate?
nodes.answer: The timing of nitrogen application from digestate is crucial as it needs to coincide with crop demand to maximize uptake efficiency and minimize environmental losses.
nodes.paragraph: Fertilization with digestate could thus increase the share of directly plant-available N, which can be field applied at the right time to meet crop demand (Fon- taine et al. 2020a, b; M ller & M ller 2012). This could increase the N uptake efficiency, contributing to improved yields and lower losses of N to the envi- ronment (DCE 2021; Fr seth et al. 2014). Harvesting of cover crops could also lead to avoided emissions from their decomposition in the field, such as ammo- nia and nitrous oxide (Fr seth et al. 2014; Nadeem et al. 2012), and leaching of nitrate, which can take place when nitrate is released at times of low crop demand (DCE 2021). The harvesting and later appli- cation of digestate could thus result in more efficient nutrient use by the crops and lower emissions to the environment. To enable continuous operation of a biogas plant, a storage solution is needed to preserve the cover crop biomass until it can be fed to the biogas reac- tor. Ensiling is a technology where the feedstock is preserved by fermentation and could be used for this purpose, which is commonly used for preservation of animal feed (Teixeira Franco et al.

nodes.label: Experimental design and 15N application
nodes.question: What was the purpose of applying low and high 15N enrichment labeling?
nodes.answer: Low 15N enrichment labeling (~ 5 at%) was used to determine fertilizer-derived plant N uptake and track the translocation of fertilizer N in the soil, while high 15N enrichment (~ 60 at%) was used for gas sampling.
nodes.paragraph: Experimental design and 15N application For each crop, 6 macroplots (WW: 3 m 8 m, SB: 3 m 11 m) were defined. Within each macroplot, a mes- oplot (1.4 m 1.4 m) and a microplot ( 30 cm) were established (Supplementary Fig. S1). In the mesoplots, we applied low 15N enrichment labeling (~ 5 at%) to determine fertilizer-derived plant N uptake and to trace translocation of fertilizer N in soil. The microplots were fertilized with high 15N enrichment (~ 60 at%) and used for gas sampling. For WW, microplots were chosen where uniformly grow - ing plants were present, for SB one representative plant was identified. Meso- and microplots remained at the same spot throughout the growing seasons. Both crops were fertilized according to their N demand and yield potential, typical for these crops in the region. WW was fertilized with 21 g N m 2 (equivalent to 210 kg N ha 1) split in two fertilizer doses of 14 g N m 2 on April 8th and 7 g N m 2 on June 11th.

nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What type of fertilizer was used for microplots and what was its composition?
nodes.answer: The microplots were fertilized with a 15N enriched tracer solution made of 15N-labeled Ca(NO3)2, which contained approximately 60 at% 15N2.
nodes.paragraph: After wheat harvest, phacelia was fertilized with 3 g N m 2 on September 6th. SB was fertilized with 10 g N m 2 (equivalent to 100 kg N ha 1) split in two fertilizer doses of 5 g N m 2 each on May 20th and July 6th. Application technique and formulation of the fertilizer differed between macro-, meso-, and microplot. Microplots were fertilized with a 15N enriched tracer solu- tion made of 15N-labeled Ca(NO3)2 (~ 60 at% 15N2, Campro Scientific GmbH, Berlin, Germany) dissolved in H2Odest. To ensure homogenous label distribution in the upper 20 cm of the microplots, we aimed to completely exchange soil water inside the upper 20 cm of the microplots with the tracer solution. Based on the findings of pre-experiments with similar soil properties to the field site, the 1.6-fold of the present soil water solution was applied to replace ~ 80% of soil water with the tracer solution. The necessary amount of water was estimated based on soil water content prior to each fertilization event. The tracer solution was applied as evenly as possible with drip irrigation in intervals (15 min application, 45 min pause) using a sprinkling head with 163 sprinkling capillaries (EcoTech, Bonn, Germany) connected to a peristaltic pump (ISM444B, Ismatec, Wertheim, Ger - many) to ensure infiltration into soil.

nodes.question: How much nitrogen was applied to SB and when?
nodes.answer: SB was fertilized with a total of 10 g N m², split into two doses of 5 g N m² each, applied on May 20th and July 6th.

nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What were the five treatments applied in the fertilization experiment?
nodes.answer: The five treatments were: control treatment (CK), chemical fertilization only (CF), combination of chemical fertilizer and manure (CFM), combination of chemical fertilizers, manure, and straw (CFMS), and combination of manure and straw (MS).
nodes.paragraph: We tested the hypothesis that the rhizosphere bacterial and fungal communities would be more stable over time with organic fertilization, relative to chemical only fertilization. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Experimental site description and soil sampling The long-term fertilization experiment with a sorghum-maize cropping system began in 2011 at the Dongyang experimental station (37 33 21 N, 112 40 2 E), Shanxi Province, China. This region has an average annual temperature of 9.7 C and an average annual rainfall of 321.4 mm. The field experiment was designed by randomized block with three replicates, and each plot was 15 5 m2. Five treatments were selected: the control treatment with no addition of fertilizer, manure or straw (CK), chemical fertilization only (CF), a combination of chemical fertilizer and manure (CFM), a combination of chemical fertilizers, manure, and straw (CFMS), and a com- bination of manure and straw (MS). Urea, diammonium phos- phate, and potassium sulphate were used at the rates of 225 kg N ha 1, 75 kg P2O5 ha 1 and 75 kg K2O ha 1 each year as chemical fertilizers.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How do nano-enabled strategies, as discussed by Kay et al., aim to enhance crop nutrition and protection?
nodes.answer: Nano-enabled strategies, as discussed by Kay et al., aim to enhance crop nutrition and protection by utilizing nanotechnology to improve the efficacy of agricultural practices and reduce environmental impacts.
